citations.quote: The MBSE approach is based around the development of an Integrated Systems Model (ISM) that contains a model of the system and most of the programmatic information about the project.

The Alabama Experiment for Galactic ray In-situ Shielding (AEGIS) was a project sponsored by the Alabama Space Grant Consortium (ASGC) in which multiple universities across Alabama collaboratively design, launch and operate a CubeSat Mission.

The scientific mission consisted of launching a 6U CubeSat in cislunar space to measure the effectiveness of lunar regolithbased material as a shield of radiation in response to NASA's strategic knowledge gaps.

The science mission objectives are still being defined but consist of performing research detecting Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) in cislunar space while using a traditional launch vehicle to either low earth orbit (LEO) or to a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO).

The educational goal remained the same and consists of organizing the project such that most of the work is realized by undergraduate students with a few graduate students and faculty members providing guidance.

The leadership board, as well as various teams are scattered throughout different universities in Alabama, creating organizational and geographical barriers. Additionally, a high turnover rate of the individuals involved is expected since the design and development work are to be accomplished by undergraduates that participate in the project voluntarily or as a curricular activity.

MBSE was chosen for the ABEX (prev. AEGIS) development in response to the challenges described in the previously. This paper provides an overview of the general strategy employed to perform the systems engineering tasks in an MBSE environment and provides a more in depth look at how the programmatic elements were adapted.

The first step in the application of the MBSE methodology was to delineate what the systems engineering effort was trying to achieve and what role would the model have. The different needs were identified during the first months of the project by the management team of the project.
The model was decided to be developed using the Systems Modeling language (SysML) implemented with CATIA|NoMagic's Cameo.

The Systems Engineering team uses the model for traditional systems engineering tasks as requirement management, MOP tracking, risk management, Interface management, change management, and trade studies.
The model is organized in two general interdependent categories. The first is the modeling of the system and the second is the programmatic aspects needed by the project.
Blocks represent each component and subsystem and contain a set of values that are pertinent for that component such as mass or power consumption.

The intricacy of these relationships ranges from ensuring that the mass of a subsystem is the sum of its components to how the dimensions of a single part impact the power collection of a solar array.

The more intricate relationships will use domain specific software tools such as Excel, STK or MATLAB, which are connected to the ISM through parametric diagrams. For example, when using an Excel sheet to gather constraint inputs to the model and communicate results thereof, the sheet can be directly synced to a table in the ISM.

The behavioral representation aims at simulating the system behavior, the different mission phases, and the system states. It is this behavior to which the constraints will react to. The behavior is represented by a set of diagrams and simulated within Cameo with Cameo Simulation Toolkit Plug-in.

To represent distinct design alternatives, the use of instances is employed. Instances contain specifications of each alternative. Once an instance is created, it is possible to apply the constraints and observe how the system would react during the simulated mission

it was decided to emulate NASA systems engineering practices as described in the systems engineering handbook [3]. The systems engineering handbook describes a set of technical and systems engineering processes. This description was used as the starting point for the generation of programmatic information in the ISM.

These needs come from three main sources: functional, science and stakeholder requirements. Functional requirements are created based on the elements describing the behavior of the system evoked in section IV of this paper. Science Requirements are sourced from the science team of the project.

Each requirement document is translated into a set of requirement elements which is in turn traced to an ABEX requirement. This allows for the verification of the compliance to the different requirements documents.
Additionally, requirements can be verified dynamically with constraints which allow verification of the compliance of the requirements through the execution of the behavior.

By creating the WBS, assigning responsibility, and tracking the progress of work completed against the schedule in the ISM, all teams can easily understand their progress as well as future plans for ABEX. The WBS is linked to a set of spreadsheets that are then sent to the different teams.

The model-based approach reduces schedule impacts of the traditional by reducing the number of channels proposed changes go through, executing engineering analysis and simulation simultaneously, allowing for reuse of existing models and automating document generation [4].

It is to be noted that most of the model structure was general and the change of mission from AEGIS to ABEX resulted in most cases in just a change of the instances used rather than modification of the structural elements.

Currently the software is planned to be generated through an export of a section of the model to be converted into an XML specification to then be used by F prime for software generation. An issue encountered was the fact that SysML and the interpreter tool, in this case CATIA NoMagic's Cameo, is not widely available and there are not many individuals proficient in it to take advantage of all the capabilities of the tool.

Only the Systems Engineering team and a few other individuals interact with the ISM directly, everyone else interacts with it using Excel spreadsheets which are in turn synchronized to element of the ISM.

Although MBSE aims at the elimination of unnecessary paper documents, there are some documents that were not able to be described in the ISM. The project management plan and the systems engineering management plan are two notable examples.
A noticeable capability deficiency of the ISM is the inability to handle spatial interfaces. Such interfaces are managed using CAD software to ensure fit.
AEGIS passed SRR in May 2020, at SRR the general systems engineering strategy in this paper was presented and refined.

Due to the revectoring of the mission, the model underwent changes to allow for the modeling of the mission and the corresponding structural changes. The MBSE implementation allowed to reuse most of the work for AEGIS.
The model is currently being integrated with first order tools by each technical team to allow for the sizing of the spacecraft given some initial parameters.
Due to the high turnover rate mentioned previously, more time needs to be spent to determine what would be the best turnover procedure for management of the ISM.

citations.quote: NASA's traditional, document-based approach to change management involves a time-consuming process that iteratively evaluates proposed changes, moving through six parties, four of which involve multiple people and actions [4]. The traceability between requirements, design, analysis and test results is difficult to maintain as many documents spread across multiple parties contain this data [4].
This allows for ease of data transfer flow in and out of the model to the relevant teams.
A change in the source requirement can be easily propagated through the system and having the source of every requirement ensures that there are no unnecessary requirements.
